questions.question: The basic structural and functional unit of the body is:
questions.explanation: Cell is the smallest living unit of the body.

questions.question: The control center of the cell is:
Cell membrane is mainly composed of:
The largest organ of the body is:
Number of bones in adult human body:
The longest bone in human body is:
The smallest bone in human body is:
Vertebral column is made up of:
The main buffering system in blood:
Hair and nails are made of:
Human body temperature is regulated by:
Final waste product of protein metabolism:
Final function of anatomy & physiology study:
Which cell organelle is primarily responsible for detoxification of drugs and alcohol?
questions.explanation: Smooth ER contains enzymes for lipid synthesis and detoxification. Ribosomes synthesize proteins, Golgi packages, lysosomes digest.

questions.question: In a cell, which structure prevents the autodigestion of the pancreas by its own enzymes?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes are stored as inactive zymogens in granules. Lysosomes are digestive, peroxisomes handle oxidative reactions, tight junctions seal cells.

questions.question: The extracellular matrix of connective tissue is composed mainly of:
options: Collagen and elastin fibers in ground substance
questions.answer: Collagen and elastin fibers in ground substance
questions.explanation: Extracellular matrix consists of protein fibers (collagen, elastin) embedded in ground substance. Keratin is epithelial, actin/myosin are muscle, phospholipid bilayer is membrane.

questions.question: Which type of epithelial tissue is adapted for secretion and absorption and is found in the stomach lining?
questions.explanation: Simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestines, specialized for secretion (mucus) and absorption. Transitional is in urinary bladder, simple squamous in alveoli, stratified squamous in skin.

questions.question: Damage to which cranial nerve would result in loss of the sense of smell?
questions.explanation: Cranial nerve I is olfactory, responsible for smell. Optic is vision, oculomotor controls eye movement, trigeminal is facial sensation and chewing.

questions.question: A patient with a lesion in the Broca's area will most likely present with:
questions.explanation: Broca's area (frontal lobe) controls speech production; damage causes expressive aphasia (difficulty speaking). Fluent meaningless speech is Wernicke's aphasia, inability to understand is receptive aphasia.

questions.question: The neurotransmitter primarily involved in muscle contraction at the neuromuscular junction is:
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is released from motor neurons and binds to receptors on muscle fibers to trigger contraction. Dopamine, serotonin, GABA are CNS neurotransmitters.

questions.question: Which part of the brain is responsible for temperature regulation, thirst, and sleep-wake cycles?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamus is the body's thermostat and regulates homeostasis, thirst, and circadian rhythms. Medulla controls vital autonomic functions, thalamus relays sensory information, cerebellum coordinates movement.

questions.question: A patient has damage to the left optic tract. What visual field defect is expected?
questions.explanation: The left optic tract carries fibers from the right visual field of both eyes; damage causes loss of right half of vision in both eyes (contralateral to lesion). Left homonymous would be right tract lesion. Bitemporal is optic chiasm lesion.

questions.question: Dermatomes are clinically useful to assess the integrity of:
questions.explanation: A dermatome is an area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve. Testing pinprick sensation maps spinal nerve function. Motor nerves are tested by muscle strength, cranial nerves by specific tests, autonomic by functions like sweating.

questions.question: The bone that does not articulate with any other bone and serves as an attachment for tongue muscles is the:
questions.explanation: The hyoid bone is unique as it floats in the neck, anchored by muscles, supports tongue and swallowing. Mandible articulates with temporal bone, vertebrae articulate with each other, stapes articulates with incus.

questions.question: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus can damage which nerve?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus; injury causes deltoid paralysis and loss of shoulder abduction. Radial nerve injury occurs in midshaft fractures, median nerve at wrist, ulnar nerve at elbow.

questions.question: Which of the following is a sesamoid bone that protects the tendon from wear?
questions.explanation: The patella (kneecap) is a sesamoid bone that develops within the quadriceps tendon, reducing friction. Calcaneus is heel bone, talus is ankle bone, navicular is tarsal bone.

questions.question: The type of joint that allows movement in all axes (multiaxial) is:
questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) allow flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and rotation. Hinge is uniaxial, pivot is rotation only, saddle is biaxial.

questions.question: The sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells is specialized for:
questions.explanation: Sarcoplasmic reticulum stores and releases calcium ions needed for muscle contraction. Mitochondria produce ATP, ribosomes synthesize protein, glycogen is stored in cytoplasm.

questions.question: Which protein binds calcium to initiate contraction in skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Calcium binds to troponin C, causing conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin. Tropomyosin blocks the site at rest. Actin and myosin are the contractile filaments.

questions.question: A patient with a lesion in the cerebellum would most likely exhibit:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar disorders cause incoordination, intention tremor (worsens with movement), and gait ataxia. Resting tremor is Parkinson's (basal ganglia), rigidity is extrapyramidal, loss of consciousness is brainstem/reticular formation.

questions.question: The foramen magnum of the skull transmits which structure?
questions.explanation: The foramen magnum is the opening at the base of the skull through which the medulla oblongata connects to the spinal cord. The spinal cord begins below the foramen magnum, pons is above, cerebellum is in posterior fossa.

questions.question: The main pacemaker of the heart, the SA node, is located in the:
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node is in the upper right atrium near the entry of the superior vena cava. It generates impulses that spread through atria. AV node is in interatrial septum, ventricles have Purkinje fibers.

questions.question: During isovolumetric contraction of the ventricles:
options: AV valves are closed, semilunar valves are closed
questions.answer: AV valves are closed, semilunar valves are closed
questions.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction is the phase when ventricles begin to contract, raising pressure, closing AV valves before semilunar valves open. Thus, all four valves are momentarily closed, volume constant.

questions.question: A patient with aortic regurgitation would have which characteristic blood pressure change?
questions.explanation: Aortic regurgitation causes backflow into left ventricle during diastole, leading to high systolic and low diastolic pressure, thus a wide pulse pressure (e.g., 160/50 mmHg). Narrow pulse pressure is seen in cardiac tamponade.

questions.question: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from placenta to the fetus?
questions.explanation: Umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from placenta to fetal liver and heart. Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from fetus to placenta. Ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale are fetal shunts.

questions.question: The foramen ovale in the fetal circulation connects:
options: Umbilical vein to inferior vena cava
questions.explanation: Foramen ovale is an opening between right and left atria in the fetus, allowing blood to bypass the non-functioning lungs. It closes after birth. Ductus arteriosus connects pulmonary artery to aorta.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin can cross the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus?
questions.explanation: Only IgG antibodies can cross the placenta, providing the newborn with temporary passive immunity. IgA is in secretions, IgM is first response and too large, IgE is for allergies.

questions.question: The primary site of haematopoiesis in adults is:
questions.explanation: In adults, hematopoiesis occurs mainly in the red marrow of flat bones (sternum, pelvis, ribs). In fetal life, liver and spleen are sites. Lymph nodes produce lymphocytes.

questions.question: A patient with blood group AB positive can donate to a recipient with blood group:
questions.explanation: AB+ individuals have both A and B antigens and Rh antigen; they can only donate to other AB+ recipients (universal recipient for blood, but not plasma). They can receive from all. O- is universal donor.

questions.question: The intrinsic pathway of coagulation is triggered by:
questions.explanation: The intrinsic pathway is initiated when blood contacts damaged vessel wall collagen, activating factor XII. Tissue factor (factor III) initiates the extrinsic pathway. Thrombin and fibrinogen are later components.

questions.question: A patient has a deficiency of factor VIII. The condition is known as:
questions.explanation: Factor VIII deficiency causes Hemophilia A (classic hemophilia). Factor IX deficiency is Hemophilia B. Von Willebrand disease involves vWF factor, thrombocytopenia is low platelets.

questions.question: The layer of the vessel wall that is primarily composed of smooth muscle and allows vasoconstriction is:
questions.explanation: Tunica media contains smooth muscle and elastic fibers responsible for vasoconstriction and vasodilation. Tunica intima is the inner endothelial layer, adventitia is outer connective tissue.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of cardiac muscle but not skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle fibers are connected by intercalated discs containing gap junctions for electrical coupling, allowing syncytium. Skeletal muscle lacks these, is multinucleated and voluntary; T-tubules are at A-I junction in skeletal, Z line in cardiac.

questions.question: During the respiratory cycle, intrapleural pressure is always:
options: Less than intrapulmonary pressure only during inspiration
questions.explanation: Intrapleural pressure is normally subatmospheric (negative) due to opposing recoil of lungs and chest wall, preventing lung collapse. It becomes more negative during inspiration but remains negative throughout.

questions.question: The majority of carbon dioxide is transported in blood as:
questions.explanation: About 70% of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate (HCO3-) after conversion by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs. 23% as carbaminohemoglobin, 7% dissolved.

questions.question: A patient with metabolic acidosis will compensate by:
questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis stimulates respiratory compensation: increased rate and depth of breathing (Kussmaul respirations) to blow off CO2 and raise pH. Hypoventilation compensates for alkalosis. Renal compensation is slower.

questions.question: The enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II is primarily found in the:
questions.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is abundant on the surface of pulmonary capillary endothelial cells. Renin is from kidney, angiotensinogen from liver, aldosterone from adrenal cortex.

questions.question: Which part of the nephron is impermeable to water but actively transports sodium and chloride?
options: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.answer: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+/K+/2Cl- but is water-impermeable, creating the medullary concentration gradient. Collecting duct permeability depends on ADH.

questions.question: The presence of protein in urine indicates damage to which structure?
questions.explanation: Proteinuria suggests increased permeability of the glomerular basement membrane, often due to glomerulonephritis. Normal glomerulus prevents large proteins from passing.

questions.question: Renin is secreted by which cells in response to low blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole secrete renin when blood pressure drops. Macula densa senses NaCl concentration, podocytes form filtration slits, mesangial cells support.

questions.question: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption in the:
questions.explanation: ADH acts on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2 channels to increase water permeability and concentrate urine. Proximal tubule reabsorbs ~65% isotonically, loop of Henle creates gradient.

questions.question: Which hormone is secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets?
questions.explanation: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, raising blood glucose. Beta cells secrete insulin, delta cells somatostatin, F cells pancreatic polypeptide.

questions.question: Cushing's syndrome is caused by excess of:
questions.explanation: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged high cortisol levels, causing weight gain, buffalo hump, striae. Excess mineralocorticoids cause Conn's syndrome, excess growth hormone causes acromegaly.

questions.question: Which of the following hormones is lipid-soluble and binds to intracellular receptors?
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones (lipophilic) cross the plasma membrane and bind to nuclear receptors. Insulin, adrenaline, glucagon are water-soluble peptide/amine hormones that bind to cell surface receptors.

questions.question: The hormone melatonin is secreted by the:
questions.explanation: Pineal gland produces melatonin, regulating sleep-wake cycles. Adrenal medulla produces adrenaline, anterior pituitary produces tropic hormones, posterior pituitary stores oxytocin and ADH.

questions.question: A patient with hyperparathyroidism will likely have:
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium (by bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and vitamin D activation) and decreases phosphate by increasing renal excretion.

questions.question: The first phase of gastric secretion, the cephalic phase, is initiated by:
options: Thought, smell, or sight of food
Presence of acid in the duodenum
questions.answer: Thought, smell, or sight of food
questions.explanation: Cephalic phase is a vagally mediated response to anticipation of food, increasing gastric acid secretion. Gastric phase responds to food in stomach, intestinal phase to chyme in intestine.

questions.question: Which of the following is correctly absorbed in the terminal ileum via intrinsic factor?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor (secreted by parietal cells) is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Iron is absorbed in duodenum, calcium in duodenum and jejunum, glucose in jejunum.

questions.question: The gastroesophageal sphincter prevents reflux of gastric contents. Its incompetence leads to:
questions.explanation: Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) dysfunction allows acid reflux, causing GERD. Achalasia is failure of LES relaxation, pyloric stenosis is narrowing of pylorus, peptic ulcer is mucosal break.

questions.question: Bile salts are essential for digestion and absorption of:
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into micelles, aiding lipase action and absorption of fatty acids and monoglycerides. They also absorb fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.question: The wave-like muscular contractions that propel food through the gastrointestinal tract are called:
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is a coordinated, unidirectional propulsive contraction. Segmentation mixes contents, haustration is colonic mixing, pendular movement is seen in small intestine.

questions.question: Which vitamin is produced by intestinal bacteria and is crucial for coagulation?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is synthesized by gut flora and is essential for synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X. Vitamin A for vision, C for collagen, D for calcium.

questions.question: The functional unit of the liver, a six-sided structure with a central vein and portal triads, is the:
questions.explanation: The classic hepatic lobule is hexagonal with a central vein and portal triads at the corners. Acinus is the functional microvascular unit, nephron is kidney, islets are pancreas.

questions.question: The space of Disse in the liver is located between:
questions.explanation: Space of Disse is the perisinusoidal space where exchange occurs between blood sinusoids and hepatocytes. It contains stellate cells. Bile canaliculi are between adjacent hepatocytes.

questions.question: The structure that drains urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder is the:
questions.explanation: Ureters are muscular tubes that propel urine from kidney to bladder. Urethra drains bladder to exterior, collecting ducts are within kidney, renal capsule is the outer covering.

questions.question: In the male reproductive system, the tube that conveys both urine and semen is the:
questions.explanation: The male urethra passes through the prostate and penis, carrying both urine and semen (not simultaneously). Vas deferens carries sperm from epididymis to ejaculatory duct, ureter carries only urine.

questions.question: The corpus luteum secretes which hormone to maintain the uterine lining during early pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Progesterone from corpus luteum stabilizes the endometrium and supports early pregnancy until placenta takes over. Estrogen contributes to proliferation, LH stimulates ovulation, FSH follicle growth.

questions.question: The ampulla of the fallopian tube is the:
options: Fimbriated end opening into peritoneal cavity
questions.explanation: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the widest and longest part of the fallopian tube. The isthmus is narrow near the uterus, infundibulum has fimbriae, interstitial part passes through uterine wall.

questions.question: Spermatogenesis occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis takes place within the seminiferous tubules of the testis. Epididymis stores and matures sperm, prostate and seminal vesicles add fluid.

questions.question: The hormone that triggers ovulation is the mid-cycle surge of:
questions.explanation: A rapid rise in LH (LH surge) around day 14 of a 28-day cycle triggers ovulation. FSH stimulates follicle development, estrogen peaks before surge, progesterone increases after ovulation.

questions.question: A patient with a spinal cord transection above T6 may experience autonomic dysreflexia, which is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in spinal cord injury above T6, triggering massive sympathetic response causing severe hypertension, with baroreflex-mediated bradycardia. Hypotension with bradycardia is spinal shock.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The limbic system includes hippocampus (memory), amygdala (emotion), cingulate gyrus, hypothalamus, etc. Cerebellum is motor coordination, not part of limbic system.

questions.question: The axillary lymph nodes primarily drain lymph from the:
questions.explanation: Axillary nodes receive lymph from the upper limb, most of the breast, and superficial trunk. Inguinal nodes drain lower limb, cervical nodes drain head/neck.

questions.question: Red pulp of the spleen functions primarily in:
questions.explanation: Red pulp contains cords and sinuses that filter blood, removing old RBCs and platelets. White pulp is lymphoid tissue. Spleen does not produce bile.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic sign of upper motor neuron lesion?
questions.explanation: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions cause increased tone (spasticity), hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign. Lower motor neuron lesions cause flaccid paralysis, atrophy, fasciculations, and absent reflexes.

questions.question: The primary sensory receptor for touch and pressure in the skin is:
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles detect light touch and are in dermal papillae. Pacinian senses deep pressure/vibration, free nerve endings sense pain/temperature, Ruffini senses stretch.

questions.question: A patient with a fracture of the distal radius and ulna with dorsal displacement is termed:
questions.explanation: Colles' fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (
). Smith's fracture has volar displacement, Boxer's involves fifth metacarpal neck, scaphoid is carpal bone.

questions.question: The anatomical snuffbox is bounded by tendons of which muscles?
options: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
questions.answer: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
questions.explanation: The snuffbox is formed by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis (anterior) and extensor pollicis longus (posterior). Scaphoid bone is palpable here.

questions.question: Which nerve is at risk during intramuscular injection in the gluteal region if incorrectly placed?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve runs through the gluteal region, and injections in the lower medial quadrant can damage it, causing foot drop. Femoral and obturator are in anterior thigh, pudendal in perineum.

questions.question: The popliteal lymph nodes drain lymph from the:
questions.explanation: Popliteal nodes behind the knee drain the lower leg and foot, then drain to deep inguinal nodes. Axillary nodes drain upper limb.

questions.question: A patient with loss of sensation on the palmar surface of the thumb, index, and middle finger likely has damage to which nerve?
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar aspect of thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger. Ulnar supplies medial half of ring and little finger, radial supplies dorsal lateral palm.

questions.question: The great saphenous vein drains into the:
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body, ascends medially to drain into the femoral vein in the femoral triangle. Small saphenous drains into popliteal vein.

questions.question: Which of the following brain structures produces cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation: CSF is secreted by the choroid plexus in the ventricles. Arachnoid villi absorb CSF into venous sinuses, dura and pia are meningeal layers.

questions.question: A patient with a basilar skull fracture may present with CSF rhinorrhea, indicating communication with which space?
questions.explanation: CSF rhinorrhea indicates a dural tear allowing leakage of CSF from the subarachnoid space into the nasal cavity. Subdural and epidural are potential spaces.

questions.question: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery arises from the maxillary artery (branch of external carotid) and enters the skull through foramen spinosum. It is frequently torn in epidural hematoma.

questions.question: Which valve is located between the left ventricle and the aorta?
questions.explanation: The aortic valve (semilunar) guards the opening from left ventricle to aorta. Mitral valve is between left atrium and ventricle, tricuspid on right side, pulmonary valve between right ventricle and pulmonary trunk.

questions.question: A thrombus formed in the left atrium in atrial fibrillation can most likely embolize to the:
questions.explanation: Left atrial thrombi can enter systemic circulation, often travelling to the brain causing stroke. Right-sided emboli go to lungs.

questions.question: The mediastinum contains all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity containing heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, thymus, etc. The lungs are in the pleural cavities, lateral to mediastinum.

questions.question: The phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm, arises from spinal cord segments:
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve originates from C3, C4, C5 (
). It provides motor innervation to the diaphragm.

questions.question: The muscle responsible for abduction of the arm (0-15°) is the:
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of abduction; deltoid continues from 15° onward. Infraspinatus is a lateral rotator, trapezius elevates and rotates scapula.

questions.question: A patient presents with numbness of the medial forearm and hand, and clawing of the ring and little fingers. The likely nerve injury is:
questions.explanation: Ulnar nerve injury leads to claw hand (hyperextension at MCP, flexion at IP of ring and little fingers), sensory loss over medial hand and forearm. Median nerve causes ape hand, radial nerve wrist drop.

questions.question: The venous angle formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins is the site of drainage of the:
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct drains lymph from most of the body into the left venous angle. Right lymphatic duct drains into right venous angle. Azygos vein drains into SVC.

questions.question: The round ligament of the liver is a remnant of the:
questions.explanation: The round ligament (ligamentum teres) is the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein. Ductus venosus becomes ligamentum venosum, ductus arteriosus becomes ligamentum arteriosum, urachus becomes median umbilical ligament.

questions.question: In portal hypertension, blood can bypass the liver via portosystemic anastomoses. Esophageal varices involve anastomosis between which veins?
questions.explanation: Esophageal varices form when portal blood from left gastric vein (portal) shunts into esophageal veins draining into azygos system (systemic). Caput medusae is paraumbilical-epigastric, hemorrhoids are rectal anastomoses.

questions.question: The Peyer's patches, aggregates of lymphoid tissue, are found in which part of the intestine?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are concentrated in the submucosa of the ileum and function in immune surveillance. They are visible as lymph nodules.

questions.question: Which of the following is a retroperitoneal organ?
questions.explanation: Kidneys are retroperitoneal, lying behind the peritoneum along with duodenum (2nd-4th parts), pancreas, ascending/descending colon. Stomach, spleen, transverse colon are intraperitoneal.

questions.question: The ureters cross the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of which artery?
questions.explanation: The ureters pass over the pelvic brim anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, then run into the pelvis. This is a key anatomical landmark.

questions.question: A patient with damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve will present with:
questions.explanation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus) innervates most laryngeal muscles; injury causes vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness. Swallowing and taste involve other nerves.

questions.question: The canal of Schlemm is involved in drainage of:
questions.explanation: Aqueous humor drains from anterior chamber through trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal, then to episcleral veins. Blockage increases intraocular pressure (glaucoma).

questions.question: The macula lutea of the retina is specialized for:
questions.explanation: Macula lutea contains the fovea centralis, packed with cones for sharp central vision and color perception. Rods are for peripheral and night vision.

questions.question: The organ of Corti is located in which cochlear duct?
questions.explanation: The organ of Corti, the sensory epithelium for hearing, rests on the basilar membrane within the scala media (endolymph-filled). Scala vestibuli and tympani contain perilymph.

questions.question: Which ossicle of the middle ear is directly attached to the tympanic membrane?
questions.explanation: The malleus (hammer) handle is embedded in the tympanic membrane. It articulates with incus (anvil), which connects to stapes (stirrup) at the oval window.

questions.question: The primary auditory cortex is located in which lobe of the brain?
questions.explanation: Auditory cortex is in the superior temporal gyrus (Heschl's gyri). Frontal lobe is motor/executive, parietal sensory, occipital visual.

questions.question: A patient with a pituitary tumor compressing the optic chiasm typically develops:
questions.explanation: The decussating nasal retinal fibers carrying temporal visual fields are damaged at the chiasm, causing loss of both temporal visual fields. Unilateral optic nerve lesion causes total blindness in that eye.

questions.question: The adrenal cortex produces all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is produced by the adrenal medulla. Adrenal cortex synthesizes corticosteroids: cortisol (zona fasciculata), aldosterone (zona glomerulosa), androgens (zona reticularis).

questions.question: The QRS complex on an ECG represents:
questions.explanation: QRS complex indicates ventricular depolarization (contraction). P wave is atrial depolarization, T wave ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization is hidden in QRS.

questions.question: Which wave on ECG is typically elevated in hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia causes tall, peaked T waves, eventually widening of QRS and loss of P waves. U wave is seen in hypokalemia.

questions.question: The peripheral chemoreceptors that respond to low oxygen are mainly located in the:
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors in carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic bodies (vagus nerve) detect decreased PaO2, increased CO2 and H+. Central chemoreceptors in medulla respond to CO2/pH.

questions.question: An anion gap metabolic acidosis with normal chloride is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: DKA increases anion gap due to ketone bodies. Diarrhea and RTA cause normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. Acetazolamide causes bicarbonate loss, also non-anion gap.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the liver related to bilirubin metabolism?
options: Conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid
questions.answer: Conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid
questions.explanation: Liver conjugates unconjugated bilirubin to make it water-soluble for biliary excretion. Urobilinogen is formed in intestines, stercobilin in feces, deamination is also liver function but not specifically bilirubin metabolism.

questions.question: The Frank-Starling law of the heart states that:
options: Heart rate increases with venous return
Stroke volume increases with increased end-diastolic volume
Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume
Blood pressure is directly proportional to peripheral resistance
questions.answer: Stroke volume increases with increased end-diastolic volume
questions.explanation: Frank-Starling mechanism: greater ventricular filling (preload) stretches cardiac muscle, leading to stronger contraction and increased stroke volume, up to a limit. It's not rate-dependent but length-dependent.

questions.question: In the nephron, the highest concentration of glucose reabsorption occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Virtually all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule via SGLT2 and SGLT1. Later segments only reabsorb scant amounts if any.

questions.question: The Hutchinson's triad (notched teeth, interstitial keratitis, deafness) is a sign of:
questions.explanation: Hutchinson's triad indicates late congenital syphilis. Rubella causes cataract, deafness, heart defects. Cerebral palsy is a motor disorder, tuberculosis doesn't present this triad.
